show_hn.story_text: I have been building realtime multiplayer games that run in a browser since 1999 and my latest is pewpewpew.io which combines everything I know about doing this well. The game uses a fully client and server synchronized state machine running at 60hz with rollback / rollforward on both client and server. During normal play only user input is transmitted using a compressed message format, where input is 7 fields in 2 bytes, with a total of about 26KB/s used for a room with 32 active players. Users are automatically distributed into a room on a server with the lowest measured ping where there are other players playing. If you've pointed Claude Code, Cursor, or OpenCode at a codebase you care about and walked away thinking AI coding tools are a net negative, I pretty much agree with you. Left directly on a working branch, models optimize for shutting the compiler up on the current turn. Hit a tricky failure and they delete the failing assertion, return a hardcoded nil/true stub, rewrite the spec to match broken code, dump a 300-line function into the wrong package, or burn $15 of tokens editing in circles. Writing longer rules files ("IMPORTANT: NEVER DELETE TESTS") breaks down once context fills up.
